title: The Last Hour Before Bed
intro: Text 1 is a poster put up by student peer helpers during the examination period.

visual.text: The last hour before bed decides the first paper tomorrow.
Close the book. Dim the screen. Let your brain file what you learnt.

A picture in two halves. On the left, a girl is hunched over her desk at 1 am, with three empty coffee cans beside her. On the right, the same girl is asleep in a dark room, her notes stacked and her school bag packed by the door.

It feels responsible to squeeze in one more chapter at midnight. It is not. While you sleep, your brain sorts and stores what you studied; cut the sleep short and much of the day’s work is never put away. Tired students misread questions and blank on formulas they knew.

visual.title: Your last hour
items: 60 minutes to go — stop new topics; skim your own summary once
45 minutes — pack your bag: entry proof, pens, calculator
30 minutes — phone on the charger, outside your room

visual.text: “I used to study until 2 am and feel proud. My marks went up the term I started sleeping at eleven.” — Daniel, 16
Cannot sleep because of worry? Talk to a Peer Support Leader or the school counsellor in the Quiet Room, open every recess.

text2.intro: Text 2 is taken from a blog post by a student who changed her study habits.
paragraphs: For most of last year, I was the friend who sent messages at 2 am asking if anyone else was still awake. I thought staying up proved I was serious. Then came the morning of my mid-year paper. In the very first question I read ‘radius’ as ‘diameter’, and I could not recall a formula I had copied out twenty times the night before. I stared at the page while the clock moved on without me.

After that, my mother and I made a deal. My phone sleeps in the kitchen, and I stop starting new topics after ten. The first week was hard; lying in the dark felt like wasting time. But in the next round of tests, I finished early enough to check my working, and I actually remembered what I had revised. I still work hard. I just stop before my brain does.

questions.text: Look at Text 1. Which sentence best states the main message of the poster?

options.label: A
options.text: Studying late at night shows that you take your exams seriously.

options.label: B
options.text: Resting well the night before is part of doing well in the exam.

options.label: C
options.text: Students should drink less coffee during the exam period.

scheme.answer: Resting well the night before is part of doing well in the exam.

questions.text: How do the two halves of the picture in Text 1 support the message of the poster?

scheme.answer: The left half shows the girl exhausted at her desk at 1 am with empty coffee cans, while the right half shows her asleep with her notes and bag ready, so the contrast shows that preparing early and sleeping is the better choice.
accept: The picture compares a tired girl studying very late with the same girl resting after getting ready, showing readers that sleep, not late-night studying, is the right way to end the day before a paper.

seeds.text: On the left she is studying at 1 am with coffee cans and looks very tired, but on the right she is sleeping with her bag already packed. The contrast shows sleeping is better than staying up, which is what the poster wants students to do.
One side shows her worn out from staying up late and the other shows her resting after getting everything ready, so it compares the bad habit with the good one the poster is telling us to follow.
It shows that students should not drink coffee because it is bad for health.
The two halves show the same girl in two different places.
On the left, a girl is hunched over her desk at 1 am, with three empty coffee cans beside her.
